purpose: Adalimumab-afzb is used to treat several conditions where your immune system is overactive and causing inflammation, such as rheumatoid arthritis, psoriatic arthritis, plaque psoriasis, Crohn's disease, and ulcerative colitis. It can help reduce pain, swelling, and other symptoms so you can feel better and stay more active. It is a biosimilar, meaning it works just like the original brand-name medicine Humira.
how_it_works: Your immune system makes a protein called TNF (tumor necrosis factor) that can cause harmful inflammation when there is too much of it. This medicine attaches to that protein and blocks it, like putting a cap on it so it cannot cause damage. By calming down that overactive signal, your body has less inflammation and your symptoms improve.
common_side_effects: The most common side effects include redness, pain, swelling, or itching at the injection site where you give yourself the shot. You may also notice headaches, a runny nose, or upper respiratory infections like a cold. Some people experience nausea or a rash.
warnings: This medicine lowers your immune system, so it is easier to get serious infections, including tuberculosis (TB). Your doctor will test you for TB before you start. Tell your doctor right away if you get a fever, chills, cough, or feel unusually tired. It may also raise the risk of certain cancers, especially lymphoma. Do not use this medicine if you have an active infection. Talk to your doctor about all vaccines before starting, as some vaccines cannot be given while on this medicine.
typical_dosing: This medicine is given as an injection under the skin (subcutaneous injection). The dose and how often you take it depends on the condition being treated — for example, for rheumatoid arthritis it is often 40 mg every other week. Your doctor or nurse will show you exactly how to inject it at home. Always follow your doctor's specific instructions for your dose and schedule.
